title: Cog
text: Cog Cog (Cloud On Go) is a file storage and plugin platform written in Go. It provides WebDAV, SFTP, and web-based file access with built-in apps for calendars, contacts, notes, tasks, RSS feeds, photo galleries, and bookmarks. Cog maintains API compatibility with NextCloud clients and ecosystem apps. For users and administrators Getting Started -- install and configure Cog Administration -- manage users, groups, volumes, and server settings Using Cog -- file management, sharing, WebDAV, SFTP, and more Apps -- built-in apps: calendar, contacts, notes, tasks, RSS, gallery, bookmarks NextCloud Compatibility -- supported APIs and tested clients For plugin developers Plugin Development -- build plugins that extend Cog with new features

title: Configuration
text: Configuration Cog reads its settings from a configuration file, which setup writes, and from environment variables, which override the file. Everything has a default that suits trying Cog out in a folder. The configuration file Setup writes cog.toml in the folder it installs to. Cog finds it: from --config <file> on the command line (the service passes this); else from COG_CONFIG; else beside an installed program: <folder>/cog.toml for <folder>/bin/cog, so admin commands run from the folder need nothing. Without one, Cog uses the defaults and the environment, as before. A setting Cog does not know is an error, so a misspelling does not go unnoticed. Edit the file and restart Cog, or run setup again, which keeps settings it does not ask about. The file is readable only by its owner: it can hold DNS credentials. Environment variables Variable Default Description COG_ADDR :8580 HTTP listen address COG_DB system.db Path to the system SQLite database COG_DATA_DIR data Root directory for user data COG_BASE_URL http://<hostname>:8580 Public URL used for generating links and login flows COG_LOG_FORMAT text Log format: text or json COG_LOG_LEVEL info Log level: debug, info, warn, error COG_SSH_ADDR :8522 SSH/SFTP listen address COG_SSH_ENABLED true Enable the SSH/SFTP server COG_SSH_HOST_KEY (auto-generated) Path to SSH host key file COG_SSH_NO_ACCOUNT_PASSWORDS false SSH takes keys and app passwords only COG_CONFIG Configuration file COG_TLS_MODE acme, files or self-signed to serve HTTPS COG_TLS_ADDR :8443 HTTPS listen address COG_TLS_HTTP_ADDR Plain HTTP listener for http-01 and redirects COG_TLS_DOMAINS Names for the certificate, comma-separated COG_TLS_EMAIL Email for the ACME account COG_TLS_CHALLENGE tls-alpn-01 tls-alpn-01, http-01 or dns-01 COG_TLS_DNS_PROVIDER DNS provider for dns-01; its credentials use lego's variables (CLOUDFLARE_DNS_API_TOKEN, DUCKDNS_TOKEN, ...) COG_TLS_CA Let's Encrypt ACME directory URL, or staging COG_TLS_CERT, COG_TLS_KEY Certificate files for files mode COG_UPDATE_CHECK true Check for releases daily COG_UPDATE_AUTO false Install releases when found Directory layout Cog organizes data under the COG_DATA_DIR directory: Key points: Each user gets an isolated directory with their own SQLite databases. Files are stored flat on disk with their original names. You can copy files directly into a user's files/ directory and Cog will detect them automatically. Plugin data is isolated per-user in app_data/<plugin_id>/. System database The system.db (path set by COG_DB) stores global state: users, sessions, groups, shares, and plugin settings. This file is separate from user data. Production deployment cog setup is the simplest route. Without it, set at minimum: See Reverse Proxy for putting Cog behind nginx or Caddy.

title: First Run
text: First Run Sign in When setup finishes it shows Open Cog. Sign in with the admin account you made. The dashboard shows an app for each enabled plugin. If Cog is reachable from the internet, do these first: Settings > Security: turn on two-factor sign-in. Settings > Security: add an SSH key if you use SFTP or rsync, and app passwords for the Nextcloud desktop and phone apps. Admin > Users: add the people who will use Cog. Where things are Everything is in the folder you chose in setup: Back up the whole folder. See Backup and Restore. Stopping and starting Setup installed a service, so Cog starts by itself. To stop or restart it: For me System service Linux systemctl --user restart cog sudo systemctl restart cog macOS launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/us.duckfam.cog sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/us.duckfam.cog Windows Task Scheduler, task Cog Services, Cog Its log is in journalctl --user -u cog (or -u cog for the system service) on Linux, cog.log in the folder on macOS, and Event Viewer on Windows. Admin > Logs shows recent entries on every platform. The command line The installed program finds its settings on its own, so admin commands work from the folder's bin: For a system service, run them as its account so files it makes belong to the server: sudo -u cog /opt/cog/bin/cog user list. Without setup To run Cog in the foreground with no service, in the current folder: It listens on :8580 (HTTP) and :8522 (SSH), keeps system.db and data/ in the current folder, and is configured with environment variables. Enable or disable apps Admin > Plugins turns apps on and off. Dashboard and Files are always on. Next steps Reaching Cog from anywhere Updates CLI Reference Email Setup -- for password resets and email codes

title: Installation
text: Installation Cog is one program. Download it, run it, and setup takes care of the rest: where it lives, the admin account, starting with your computer, and, if you want it, reaching it from anywhere over HTTPS. Download Get the file for your computer from the releases page: Computer File Windows (most PCs) cog-windows-amd64.exe Mac with Apple silicon (M1 and later) cog-darwin-arm64 Mac with an Intel processor cog-darwin-amd64 Linux on a PC cog-linux-amd64 Linux on a Raspberry Pi 4/5 or other 64-bit ARM cog-linux-arm64 Run setup Windows Double-click cog-windows-amd64.exe. Setup opens in your browser. The first time, Windows SmartScreen may say it protected your PC from an unrecognised app: choose More info, then Run anyway. When Cog first listens on the network, Windows Firewall asks whether to allow it; allow it on private networks, and on public ones too if you will forward ports to it. macOS Double-click the file. macOS opens it in Terminal, and setup opens in your browser. Downloaded programs that are not from the App Store are blocked the first time. Open System Settings > Privacy & Security, find the message about cog-darwin-arm64 near the bottom, and choose Open Anyway. Or, in Terminal: Linux With a desktop, setup opens in your browser; over SSH or on a server with no desktop, it asks its questions in the terminal. --cli and --web choose one or the other. What setup asks Setup asks one question a page, and skips the pages your answers make unnecessary. How Cog runs. On this computer, for me starts Cog when you sign in and runs it as you, with no administrator rights: the right choice for a home computer. As a server starts it with the computer, as an account of its own, and needs an administrator's password. Where to keep your files. One folder holds Cog's program, settings and everyone's files. Pick a disk with room. Where you will use Cog from: only on this computer; at home, on your network, over plain HTTP or over HTTPS with a certificate Cog makes (browsers warn once per device; setup shows the fingerprint to compare); anywhere, on your devices with Tailscale, if Tailscale runs on this computer: no ports to open, and Tailscale Funnel if people without Tailscale need share links; anywhere, including people you share with, over HTTPS with your router forwarding ports to you; through a reverse proxy you already run. See Reaching Cog from anywhere. SFTP and SSH, and whether account passwords may sign in over it. Updates: check daily, and whether to install them automatically. The admin account you sign in with. Setup then shows your answers, each with a link to change it, and what it will do, including the port forwarding rules to add to your router. Then it does it: copies Cog into the folder, writes its settings, makes the admin account, gets a certificate, starts the service, and gives you the link to open. Running setup again Run the downloaded file again, or the installed one (bin/cog in the folder you chose), to: change any setting: setup opens on a summary of the current ones, each with a link to the question that sets it; reset an admin's password, for when you are locked out; remove the service (your files and data stay in the folder). Containers and distribution packages The container image is built without setup or the updater: you configure it with environment variables and update it by pulling a new image. To build such a binary yourself, use the nosetup build tag: go build -tags nosetup ./cmd/cog. From source Requires Go 1.26 or later and a C compiler (for SQLite). Optional tools Some features use other programs when they are installed. Run cog doctor to see which are available. Tool Used by For ffmpeg / ffprobe Gallery, Feeds Video thumbnails, metadata, media packaging LibreOffice Files Document previews tesseract Search Text in images yt-dlp Feeds Video downloads Everything else is built into the one program. Next steps First Run -- sign in and look around Configuration -- the settings file and environment variables

title: App Passwords
text: App Passwords App passwords are alternative credentials for use with third-party clients and scripts. They work anywhere your main password works (WebDAV, SFTP, API) but can be individually revoked without changing your main password. Why use app passwords Security -- if a client is compromised, revoke its app password without affecting other clients Convenience -- some clients (NextCloud desktop/mobile) create app passwords automatically via Login Flow Automation -- use app passwords in scripts and cron jobs Creating an app password Go to Settings > Security Under "App Passwords", enter a name for the new password (e.g. "laptop sync", "backup script") Click Create Copy the generated password -- it is shown only once Using app passwords App passwords work with: WebDAV -- use as the password in Basic Auth or Bearer token SFTP/SSH -- use as the password when connecting API -- use as a Bearer token in the Authorization header NextCloud clients -- Login Flow creates app passwords automatically Revoking app passwords Go to Settings > Security and click the delete button next to the app password you want to revoke. The client using that password will immediately lose access.

title: Files
text: Files The Files app is the core of Cog. It provides a web-based file browser for uploading, downloading, organizing, and sharing files. File browser Access your files at /apps/files/ after logging in. The browser supports: Upload -- drag and drop files or use the upload button. Large files are uploaded in chunks automatically. Download -- click a file to download it, or select multiple files. Create folders -- use the "New Folder" button. Rename -- click the file name to rename. Move -- drag files between folders. Delete -- select files and delete. Deleted files go to the trash. Favorites Mark files or folders as favorites for quick access. Favorites are available from the sidebar under "Favorites". Flat storage Files are stored on disk with their original names. Admins can copy files directly into a user's files/ directory on the server and Cog will detect them automatically on the next directory listing. No import scan is required. Volumes and mounts Your file tree can include other storage at folders you choose: volumes, storage shared with you, and your own WebDAV servers. See Storage. Access methods Files are accessible through multiple protocols: Web UI -- /apps/files/ WebDAV -- see WebDAV SFTP -- see SFTP Public links -- see Sharing Search Use the search bar to find files by name or content. See Search for details.

title: Groups
text: Groups A group is a set of people you share with together. Share a folder, a calendar or an address book with a group, and everyone in it gets access, including people who join later. Leaving a group, or being removed from it, takes that access away. Your groups are under Settings > Groups: the ones you own and the ones you belong to. Creating a group Type a name under Create group and click Create. You are the group's first owner. Open the group to add people. Members and owners Owners manage the group: they rename it, add and remove members, and invite people. Members are in it, and get whatever is shared with it. Add member adds someone by name straight away. Add another group as a member puts a whole group inside this one: sharing with this group shares with everyone in that one too. An owner can make a member an owner, or an owner a member, from the Role column. To leave a group, click Leave beside your own name. The last owner cannot leave: make someone else an owner first. Only an administrator can delete a group. Invitations An owner can invite someone instead of adding them, under Invitations on the group's page: With an email address, Cog emails the invitation, if the server has email set up. Without one, Cog makes a link to send yourself. Anyone with the link can join, so send it only to the person you mean. Choose whether they join as a member or an owner. Pending invitations are listed with their links; Revoke one and its link stops working. When someone invites you, the invitation shows at the top of Settings > Groups. Join it, or Decline. Sharing with a group Wherever you share, search for the group's name instead of a person's. See Sharing.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication
text: Multi-Factor Authentication Cog supports multiple MFA methods that can be enabled from Settings > Security. TOTP (Authenticator App) Time-based One-Time Passwords work with any authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, etc.). Setup Go to Settings > Security Click Set up TOTP Scan the QR code with your authenticator app Enter the 6-digit code to confirm Backup codes After enabling TOTP, you receive a set of backup codes. Store these in a safe place -- each backup code can be used once to log in if you lose access to your authenticator app. Regenerate backup codes from Settings > Security if needed. Email OTP Receive a 6-digit code via email each time you log in. Requires email to be configured on the server. Setup Ensure your account has an email address set in your profile Go to Settings > Security Click Enable Email OTP Codes expire after 10 minutes. WebAuthn / Passkeys Use hardware security keys (YubiKey) or platform authenticators (Touch ID, Windows Hello) for passwordless MFA. Setup Go to Settings > Security Click Register Passkey Follow your browser's prompts to register the device Name the passkey for identification You can register multiple passkeys and remove individual ones. Login flow with MFA Enter your username and password If MFA is enabled, you are redirected to the MFA challenge page Choose your method (TOTP, email OTP, or passkey) and verify On success, you are logged in App passwords bypass MFA -- they are intended for clients that cannot perform interactive MFA challenges.

title: SFTP
text: SFTP Cog includes a built-in SSH/SFTP server for secure file transfers. Connection Default port is 8522 (configurable via COG_SSH_ADDR). Authentication Password -- your Cog password or an app password SSH keys -- manage keys from Settings > Security in the web UI or via the SSH shell keys command SCP rsync SSH Shell Connecting via SSH opens an interactive shell: The shell provides built-in commands for browsing files, managing tasks, reading RSS feeds, and more. Plugins can register their own shell commands. Run help in the shell for available commands. The same shell is also available locally via: Disabling SSH Set COG_SSH_ENABLED=false to disable the SSH/SFTP server entirely.

title: Search
text: Search Cog provides full-text search across files and plugin data using a Bleve index. Using search Use the search bar in the navigation to search across all your data. Results include: Files -- matched by filename and text content Notes -- matched by title and body text Bookmarks -- matched by title, URL, description, and tags Calendar events -- matched by summary, description, and location Tasks -- matched by summary and description RSS articles -- matched by title and content Contacts -- matched by name, email, and phone number Media episodes -- matched by title, type, and description Results link directly to the matched item in its app. Query syntax Syntax Example Description term alice Matches any field containing the term "phrase" "hello world" Matches the exact phrase NOT / ! NOT alice Excludes matches AND alice AND bob Both terms must match (implicit when space-separated) OR alice OR bob Either term matches () (alice OR bob) AND files Group expressions :field=value :source=files Field equals value :field="value" :source="my notes" Field equals quoted value :field IN (...) :source IN (files, notes) Field matches any value in set Operator precedence From lowest to highest: OR, AND (implicit between adjacent terms), NOT/!. Available fields source -- the plugin that indexed the item (e.g. files, notes, rss, bookmarks, calendar, tasks, contacts, media) name -- the primary display name subtext -- secondary display text Examples How it works Each plugin registers a search source that tells Cog which database tables to index and how to map columns to searchable fields. Cog maintains a per-user Bleve index that is updated asynchronously when data changes. Eventual consistency Search indexing is asynchronous. After creating or modifying content, there may be a brief delay before changes appear in search results. The index catches up automatically. Admin search Admins have access to a system-wide search at Admin > Search that can search across all users.

title: Sharing
text: Sharing Cog provides a unified sharing system for files, folders, and plugin resources (calendars, bookmarks folders, etc.). Share targets You can share with: Users -- share directly with another user on the server Groups -- share with all members of a group (including nested groups) Public link -- generate a URL that anyone can use to access the resource Permissions Shares use a permission bitmask: Permission Description Read View the resource Write Modify the resource Reshare Share the resource with others Some plugins define additional permissions (e.g., Free/Busy and Schedule for calendars). Sharing files and folders Select a file or folder in the file browser Click the share icon Search for users or groups, or create a public link Set permissions Sharing a folder grants access to all files and subfolders within it. Public links Public links allow anyone with the URL to access the shared resource without logging in. Options: Password protection -- require a password to access the link Expiration -- set an automatic expiry date Permissions -- read-only or read/write Public links are accessible at /s/<token>. Shared with me Resources shared with you appear in the relevant app. For example, shared files appear in your file browser and shared calendars appear in the calendar app. Plugin resources Plugins can register their own shareable resource types. For example: Calendars can be shared (Calendar app) Bookmark folders can be shared (Bookmarks app) Task lists can be shared (Tasks app) Photo albums can be shared (Gallery app) The sharing UI is consistent across all resource types.

title: Storage
text: Storage Settings > Storage shows how much space you use, and what else is in your files besides what you put there yourself: storage someone shared with you, and your own WebDAV servers. Usage How much you keep in Cog, and your limit if your administrator set one. It counts your files, what apps keep for you, and your calendars and contacts. Files in a mount count towards the volume they are on instead. Mounts A mount puts other storage at a folder of your choice in your files, such as /Photos/Family. Its files then show in the file browser, over WebDAV and over SFTP, like your own. There are three kinds: A volume: a whole volume, or a folder of one (the Subpath), that you own or that someone shared with you. Storage (Storage badge): space of your own on a volume an administrator set aside for that. Shared (Shared badge): a folder someone shared with you. Access says whether you can change the files or only read them. That is up to whoever shared it. Remove takes a mount out of your files. The files themselves stay where they are. Adding a mount Under Add a mount, pick the volume, type the folder to put it at (Path), and if you want only part of it, the folder inside it (Subpath). Folders shared with you, and storage shared with you, are added from Files > Shared with me instead: open the share and click Add to my files or Add storage. Your own volumes My volumes are storage you add yourself: a WebDAV server, such as another Cog, a NextCloud, or a NAS. Fill in Add a WebDAV volume with its address and how to sign in to it, then mount it under Mounts. From the list you can Browse a volume, Share it with other people or groups (they can then mount it too), or Delete it.

title: WebDAV
text: WebDAV Cog provides a WebDAV endpoint compatible with NextCloud clients and standard WebDAV tools. Endpoint Replace <username> with your Cog username. Authentication Use an app password for WebDAV clients. App passwords are recommended over your main password for third-party client access. Basic authentication and bearer tokens are both supported. Compatible clients NextCloud Desktop Client Open the NextCloud desktop client Enter your Cog server URL (e.g. https://cloud.example.com) Follow the Login Flow to authenticate The client will sync your files automatically NextCloud Mobile (Android/iOS) Add a new account Enter your Cog server URL Authenticate via Login Flow macOS Finder In Finder, press Cmd+K Enter https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/files/<username>/ Enter your username and app password Windows Explorer Right-click "This PC" > "Map network drive" Enter https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/files/<username>/ Enter credentials when prompted rclone curl Chunked uploads Cog supports the NextCloud v2 chunked upload protocol for large files. Compatible clients (NextCloud desktop/mobile) use this automatically. Direct download tokens The API supports generating short-lived direct download tokens that allow unauthenticated file access. These are used internally by NextCloud clients for preview generation.

title: Bookmarks
text: Bookmarks The Bookmarks app provides bookmark management with folders, tags, and NextCloud Bookmarks API compatibility. Features Folders -- organize bookmarks in a hierarchical folder tree Tags -- label bookmarks for filtering Search -- find bookmarks by title, URL, description, or tag Import/Export -- Netscape HTML bookmark format Favicon fetching -- automatic favicon retrieval Availability checking -- periodic checks for broken links Click tracking -- track how often you visit each bookmark Adding bookmarks Add bookmarks from the web UI or via the NextCloud Bookmarks API. Bookmarks can exist in multiple folders simultaneously. Import/Export Import bookmarks from browsers or other services using the standard Netscape HTML format. The folder hierarchy is preserved during import. Export your bookmarks in the same format for backup or migration. NextCloud Bookmarks API The Bookmarks app implements the NextCloud Bookmarks REST API v2 (/index.php/apps/bookmarks/public/rest/v2/) for compatibility with: NextCloud Bookmarks browser extensions Floccus (browser bookmark sync) Third-party bookmark managers The API supports bookmarks, folders, tags, hash-based sync, and import/export. Sharing Bookmark folders can be shared with users or groups: Read -- view bookmarks in the folder Write -- add, edit, and delete bookmarks in the folder Reshare -- manage sharing Public links create a read-only view of the folder's bookmarks. Search Bookmarks are indexed for full-text search. Search matches against title, URL, description, page content, and tags.

title: Calendar
text: Calendar The Calendar app provides event management with full CalDAV compatibility. Features Multiple calendars per user with custom names and colors Day, week, and month views Recurring events with recurrence rules (RFC 5545 RRULE) Event exceptions (modify or delete individual occurrences) Reminders All-day events Event location and description CalDAV The calendar is fully accessible via CalDAV (RFC 4791), making it compatible with: Thunderbird (built-in calendar) Apple Calendar (macOS/iOS) DAVx5 (Android) GNOME Calendar NextCloud desktop/mobile clients CalDAV URLs Discovery: /.well-known/caldav Principal: /remote.php/dav/principals/users/<username>/ Calendars: /remote.php/dav/calendars/<username>/ Events are stored as iCalendar (.ics) blobs in the database for lossless sync with CalDAV clients. Sharing Calendars can be shared with users or groups: Read -- view events Write -- add, edit, and delete events Reshare -- manage sharing Sharing a calendar grants access to all events within it. Search Calendar events are indexed for full-text search. Search by event summary, description, or location.

title: Contacts
text: Contacts The Contacts app provides address book management with full CardDAV compatibility. Features Multiple address books per user vCard storage with all standard fields (name, email, phone, address, etc.) Import and export vCards Duplicate detection Contact search CardDAV The contacts app implements CardDAV (RFC 6352) for sync with: Apple Contacts (macOS/iOS) DAVx5 (Android) Thunderbird (with CardBook or built-in) GNOME Contacts NextCloud desktop/mobile clients CardDAV URLs Discovery: /.well-known/carddav Principal: /remote.php/dav/principals/users/<username>/ Address books: /remote.php/dav/addressbooks/<username>/ Sync uses incremental sync tokens -- clients only fetch changes since their last sync. Sharing Address books can be shared with users or groups: Read -- view contacts Write -- add, edit, and delete contacts Reshare -- manage sharing Import/Export Import and export contacts in vCard format from the web UI. Search Contacts are indexed for full-text search. Search by name, email, phone number, or other vCard fields.

title: Dashboard
text: Dashboard The Dashboard is the landing page when you log into Cog. It displays an overview of your apps and recent activity. App grid The top of the dashboard shows a grid of cards linking to each enabled app (Files, Calendar, Notes, etc.). Disabled apps do not appear. Widgets Below the app grid, plugins can contribute widgets showing relevant information: Recent Files -- your most recently modified files Upcoming Events -- next calendar events Recent Bookmarks -- recently added bookmarks Other plugins may add their own widgets Widgets are ordered by priority (set by each plugin) and render server-side on each page load. Plugin management Admins can enable or disable plugins from Admin > Plugins. The Dashboard and Files plugins are protected and always enabled.

title: Gallery
text: Gallery The Gallery app provides photo and video management with automatic organization, metadata extraction, and optional image recognition. Features Timeline view -- browse photos chronologically Albums -- manual and auto-generated (by date, location, camera, folder) EXIF metadata -- view camera settings, GPS coordinates, and timestamps Video support -- thumbnails and playback (requires ffmpeg) People/faces -- face detection and clustering (optional, see Recognition below) Tags -- automatic and manual tagging Places -- browse photos by location (reverse geocoding) File renaming -- organize photos by date/location using templates Background scanning The gallery scans your files automatically in the background. It reads from the file metadata index (not the filesystem directly), so scanning is fast even for large libraries. New, changed, and deleted files are detected incrementally. Auto-albums The gallery automatically creates albums grouped by: Date -- monthly groupings Location -- city/country from GPS data Camera -- camera make and model Folder -- source directory Image recognition Optional AI-powered tagging and face detection. Configure from Gallery > Settings: Backend Description Ollama Local or remote Ollama instance with a vision model OpenAI Vision Any OpenAI-compatible API Recognition processes images in the background. Results appear as tags and face clusters that you can name and organize. File renaming Organize photos into folders based on EXIF metadata using Go template patterns: Available fields: Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second, Camera, Lens, Original, Ext, Place, Country, Width, Height. Preview changes before applying. Undo the last rename batch if needed. Video support Requires ffmpeg and ffprobe on the system. The gallery extracts video thumbnails, duration, resolution, and codec information. Videos play natively in the browser. Sharing Albums and individual photos can be shared with users, groups, or via public links. NextCloud Memories API The gallery implements the NextCloud Memories API for compatibility with the Memories app. Search Photos are indexed for search by filename and location.

title: Notes
text: Notes The Notes app provides markdown note-taking with notebooks and tags. Features Markdown editing -- write notes in GitHub-Flavored Markdown Notebooks -- organize notes into logical groups Tags -- label notes for filtering and discovery Archive -- archive notes you want to keep but hide from the main view Autosave -- notes save automatically as you type Editing The editor supports standard Markdown with: Headings, bold, italic, links, images Code blocks with syntax highlighting Lists (ordered and unordered) Tables Blockquotes Sharing Notes and notebooks can be shared with users or groups: Read -- view the note Write -- edit the note Reshare -- manage sharing Search Notes are indexed for full-text search. Search matches against note titles, body text, and tags.

title: RSS / News
text: RSS / News The RSS app provides a feed reader for subscribing to and reading RSS and Atom feeds. Features Feed subscriptions -- add RSS/Atom feed URLs Folders -- organize feeds into categories Read/unread tracking -- mark articles as read individually or in bulk Starred articles -- save important articles OPML import/export -- import and export feed subscriptions Adding feeds Go to the RSS app Click "Add Feed" Enter the RSS or Atom feed URL Optionally assign it to a folder Background polling Feeds are polled automatically in the background. The poller uses conditional HTTP requests (ETags and Last-Modified) to minimize bandwidth. Failed feeds are retried with exponential backoff. NextCloud News API The RSS app implements the NextCloud News API for compatibility with News reader apps: News API endpoint: /index.php/apps/news/api/v1-2/ Compatible clients include: NextCloud News (Android/iOS) Newsboat (with NextCloud News plugin) FeedMe (Android) Import/Export Import and export feed subscriptions in OPML format. Search RSS articles are indexed for full-text search. Search by article title or content.

title: Tasks
text: Tasks The Tasks app provides task management with CalDAV VTODO integration. Features Task lists -- organize tasks into separate lists with names and colors Subtasks -- create hierarchical task trees Due dates -- set deadlines on tasks Priorities -- mark task importance Progress tracking -- track percentage complete Drag-and-drop ordering -- reorder tasks visually CalDAV integration Task lists are exposed as CalDAV VTODO collections, compatible with: Thunderbird (Tasks) Apple Reminders (macOS/iOS) DAVx5 + OpenTasks (Android) GNOME To Do CalDAV URL Task lists appear alongside calendars at: Tasks are stored as iCalendar VTODO objects for lossless sync. Calendar view Tasks with due dates can appear on the calendar grid (if the Calendar app is enabled), giving you a unified view of events and deadlines. Sharing Task lists can be shared with users or groups: Read -- view tasks Write -- add, edit, and complete tasks Reshare -- manage sharing Sharing a task list grants access to all tasks and subtasks within it. Search Tasks are indexed for full-text search. Search by task summary or description.

title: Backup and Restore
text: Backup and Restore What to back up System database -- the file at COG_DB (default system.db). Contains users, sessions, groups, shares, and plugin settings. Data directory -- the entire COG_DATA_DIR (default data/). Contains per-user files, databases, and plugin data. These two items contain all Cog state. Back up both to fully restore a Cog instance. SQLite considerations Cog uses SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode. Each .db file may have associated -wal and -shm files. Recommended approach: Stop Cog before backing up to ensure clean database state. If you need hot backups, copy the .db, -wal, and -shm files together atomically (e.g., using filesystem snapshots or sqlite3 .backup). Do not copy only the .db file while Cog is running -- you may get a corrupt backup if there are uncommitted WAL entries. Backup script example Restore Stop Cog Replace system.db and data/ with the backup contents Start Cog Cog will run any pending migrations automatically on startup.

title: CLI Reference
text: CLI Reference Cog provides a command-line interface for server management. Running cog without arguments starts the HTTP server. Commands cog serve Start the HTTP and SSH servers. This is also the default when running cog with no subcommand. cog user Manage user accounts. cog group Manage groups. cog volume Manage storage volumes. cog setting View and modify system settings. cog user find-key Print the username that owns an SSH public key, given its SHA256 fingerprint (the %f token in sshd's AuthorizedKeysCommand). Exits non-zero if no user has the key, or if more than one user added it. cog shell Start an interactive shell session (same shell available via SSH). cog doctor Run diagnostic checks on the server and its dependencies. Reports the status of optional external tools (ffmpeg, etc.) and database integrity. Plugins can contribute their own health checks. cog setup Installs Cog as a service, or changes, resets or removes an install. In the browser when there is a desktop, else at the terminal. See Installation. cog update Installs the newest release over the running program and restarts the service. See Updates. cog version Prints the version. cog docs Builds this documentation as a static website, the same pages Cog serves at /docs/, with a search that runs in the browser. --out <folder> (default public) is replaced with the site; --serve localhost:8080 then serves it. Every command takes --config <file> to read a configuration file other than the one beside the installed program. Plugin commands Plugins can register CLI commands that appear as subcommands under their plugin ID: For example, a bookmarks plugin registering a scan command would be invoked as:

title: Email Configuration
text: Email Configuration Cog uses SMTP to send emails for password resets, email OTP codes, and notifications. Setup Configure email from the admin panel at Admin > Settings > Email. Required fields: SMTP Host -- mail server hostname (e.g. smtp.example.com) SMTP Port -- typically 587 (STARTTLS) or 465 (SSL) Username -- SMTP authentication username Password -- SMTP authentication password From Address -- sender address for outgoing emails (e.g. cog@example.com) Testing After saving SMTP settings, use the Send Test Email button on the email settings page to verify the configuration works. Email templates Cog ships with built-in email templates for: Password reset links Email OTP codes Group invitations Admins can preview email templates at Admin > Email > Preview. Features that require email Password Reset -- users can request a password reset link via email from the login page Email OTP -- two-factor authentication via emailed one-time codes (see MFA) If SMTP is not configured, these features are unavailable. Users will see a message indicating email is not set up.

title: Reaching Cog from Anywhere
headings: How Let's Encrypt checks the name is yours
On your network only, over HTTPS
text: Reaching Cog from Anywhere Cog can serve HTTPS itself, with a free certificate from Let's Encrypt that it renews on its own. This page is about the usual home setup: Cog on a computer in your house, and your router passing connections from the internet to it. Choose Anywhere, over HTTPS in setup and it does everything here except the router. If you already run Caddy, nginx or Traefik, choose through a reverse proxy I already run instead and see Reverse Proxy. If you use Tailscale, see With Tailscale: it needs no domain and no router. What you need A domain name that points at your home. Your home's public address is your router's internet (WAN) address. Most home addresses change now and then, so use a dynamic DNS service that follows it: Duck DNS and deSEC are free, and many routers can update them by themselves. If you own a domain, your DNS host may offer the same, or Cog's DNS check (below) works with it directly. Port forwarding on your router. Setup's review page lists the rules with this computer's address filled in. For the default settings: Name Protocol Public port To this computer, port Cog HTTPS TCP 443 8443 Cog SSH (optional) TCP 8522 8522 Cog listens on 8443 rather than 443 so that it needs no administrator rights; the router translates. Look for "Port forwarding", "Virtual servers" or "NAT" in the router's settings. A fixed address for this computer on your network. Routers hand out addresses that can change; make a "DHCP reservation" for this computer so the rules keep pointing at it. Some internet providers (often mobile and satellite ones, and some fibre) put many customers behind one address ("carrier-grade NAT"), and nothing from outside reaches you. If your router's WAN address starts with 100.64 to 100.127, or does not match what shows, ask your provider for a public address, or use the reverse proxy route with a tunnel such as Cloudflare Tunnel or Tailscale Funnel. How Let's Encrypt checks the name is yours Setup offers three ways, which differ in what must be reachable: Through the HTTPS port (TLS-ALPN-01, the default). Let's Encrypt connects to port 443, which your router sends to Cog. Nothing else to forward. Through port 80 (HTTP-01). For routers or providers that will not pass 443 until a certificate exists. Forward public port 80 to the computer's port 8080 too. Port 80 then also sends visitors on to HTTPS. Through your DNS host (DNS-01). Cog adds a record with your DNS host's API. No ports need forwarding for the certificate (people still need 443 to reach Cog), and it is the only way to get a wildcard certificate (*.example.com). Built in: Cloudflare, deSEC, DigitalOcean, Duck DNS, Gandi, Hetzner, Namecheap, OVH, Porkbun, RFC 2136 (BIND, Knot, PowerDNS), lego's httpreq and exec. Setup asks for the certificate before it finishes, so a mistake shows up there with what to check. If it fails, Cog still starts and tries again every hour; once the problem is fixed it serves HTTPS without being set up again. To experiment without running into Let's Encrypt's limits, tick Use Let's Encrypt's test service, then run setup again without it. With Tailscale Tailscale joins your devices into a private network. If it runs on the computer Cog is on, choose Anywhere, on my devices with Tailscale in setup. Setup runs tailscale serve, so https://<computer>.<tailnet>.ts.net reaches Cog from every device signed in to your tailnet, with a certificate Tailscale renews. Nothing is forwarded on the router and Cog listens on this computer only. Turn on HTTPS Certificates on the DNS page of Tailscale's admin console first; setup says so if it is off. On Linux, tailscale serve needs root or Tailscale's operator: for a per-user install run sudo tailscale set --operator=$USER once. Tailscale Funnel also lets in people who do not use Tailscale, which share links need. It must be allowed for the computer in the tailnet's access controls. With it on, the sign-in page is on the internet: the advice under Keeping it safe applies. Choosing something else in setup later turns tailscale serve (or Funnel) off again. On your network only, over HTTPS Choose At home, on my network, then HTTPS with a certificate Cog makes. Cog signs a certificate for this computer's address and names (192.168.1.20, homebox, homebox.local) and renews it itself. No CA vouches for it, so each browser warns the first time: setup and Cog's log show its SHA-256 fingerprint, which you compare with the one in the browser's warning before you accept it. The certificate is kept in data/tls; a new name in domains makes a new one. Keeping it safe Anyone on the internet can reach your sign-in page once the port is open. Use a long admin password and turn on two-factor sign-in (Settings > Security). Admins can require it for everyone in Admin > General. Cog limits how fast anyone can guess passwords, per address and per account, over the web, WebDAV and SSH alike. SSH: setup turns account passwords off for SSH when Cog is reachable from the internet, so it takes keys and app passwords only, which cannot be guessed. Forwarding the SSH port is optional; leave it closed if you only use SFTP at home. Keep Cog updated. Leave the daily check on; Admin > Updates installs a release with one click, or setup can install them automatically. Plain HTTP stays on, but only for this computer (127.0.0.1:8580), for the command line and anything set up to use it before. Settings Setup writes these to cog.toml; you can also set them by hand or with environment variables (see Configuration). Certificates and the ACME account are kept in data/acme. With mode = "files", Cog serves the certificate in cert_file and key_file and reloads them hourly, so a certificate another tool renews is picked up without a restart.

title: Reverse Proxy
text: Reverse Proxy Cog works behind any reverse proxy. Set COG_BASE_URL to match your public URL. Requirements Forward the Host header Forward X-Forwarded-Proto so Cog knows it's behind HTTPS Pass through WebDAV methods (PROPFIND, MKCOL, MOVE, COPY, PROPPATCH, REPORT, LOCK, UNLOCK) Do not buffer request bodies (needed for large file uploads) Caddy Caddy automatically handles TLS and forwards the required headers. nginx Traefik Environment The base URL is used for: Generating redirect URLs during login flows NextCloud Login Flow v2 grant URLs Public share links CalDAV/CardDAV service discovery

title: Updates
text: Updates Cog installed with setup keeps itself up to date. How it works Once a day Cog reads the list of releases published with this documentation (releases.json). When there is a newer one, Admin > Updates shows it, with a link to what changed, and Install and restart: downloads the new program for this computer; checks it against the checksum in the release list, and that it runs; puts it in place of the running one; restarts. The service brings Cog back on the new version within a few seconds; uploads and downloads in progress are interrupted. With Install new versions automatically (setup, or auto = true below), Cog does this as soon as it finds a release. The release list is signed. Cog only believes a list signed with the key its own build trusts, and only installs a program whose checksum the list gives, so the download location being tampered with cannot install anything. From the command line Settings When Cog cannot update itself The updater writes the new program beside the old one, so the account Cog runs as must be able to write to the bin folder. Setup arranges that. If you moved the program somewhere it cannot write, Admin > Updates says so; run cog update as an account that can, or download the release yourself. Container images and distribution packages are built without the updater: update them the way you installed them (docker pull, your package manager). Prereleases A release whose version has a suffix (v1.4.0-rc.1) is a prerelease. It is only offered to Cog that is itself running a prerelease, so to try one, install it by hand; from then on you get the next prerelease or release, whichever is newer.

title: Users and Groups
text: Users and Groups Users Creating users Create users from the CLI: Or from the web admin panel at Admin > Users > New User. User data Each user gets an isolated directory under COG_DATA_DIR: files/ -- the user's home directory (accessible via web UI, WebDAV, SFTP) app_data/ -- per-plugin databases and caches user.db -- user-scoped settings and auth state Admin privileges Admins can access the admin panel, manage other users, configure plugins, and manage system volumes. Grant admin privileges: Quotas Admins can set storage quotas per user from the admin panel at Admin > Users > Edit User. Quotas limit the total file storage for a user. Uploads that would exceed the quota are rejected. Groups Groups are collections of users, and can contain other groups. Anyone can create a group and manage the ones they own: see Groups for how owners and members use them. This section is what an administrator has besides. Managing groups Admin > Groups lists every group, whoever owns it. An administrator can manage any group as its owner would, and delete one. From the command line: Invitations by email Owners can invite people by email only when email is set up. Without it, they get a link to send themselves.

title: Volumes
text: Volumes Volumes are storage backends that can be mounted into user virtual filesystems. Volume types Scheme Description file:// Local filesystem directory webdav:// Remote WebDAV server Each user has a default local volume created automatically. Admins can create additional volumes for shared storage. Creating volumes CLI Web admin Go to Admin > Volumes to create and manage volumes. System vs user volumes System volumes are created by admins and have no owner. They can be shared with any user or group. User volumes are created by individual users from Settings > Storage for their own use (see Storage). Mounting volumes Volumes must be mounted into a user's virtual filesystem before they can access the contents. This makes the volume's contents appear at /Photos/Shared in Alice's file browser, WebDAV, and SFTP. Users mount volumes shared with them themselves: see Storage. Sharing volumes Volumes are shareable resources. Share a system volume with a group so all members can mount it: Go to Admin > Volumes Select the volume and click Share Choose users or groups and set permissions (Read, Read/Write) Each member then mounts the shared volume at their preferred location in their own VFS. Flat file storage Files within volumes are stored with their original names on disk. There is no content-addressable hashing or opaque ID renaming. Admins can copy files directly into a volume's backing directory and Cog will detect them on the next directory listing.

title: Compatible Clients
text: Compatible Clients Cog works with NextCloud clients and standard CalDAV/CardDAV apps. Use your Cog server URL wherever the client asks for a NextCloud or WebDAV server address. NextCloud Desktop Client The official NextCloud desktop sync client works with Cog for file synchronization. Download from nextcloud.com/install Enter your Cog server URL (e.g. https://cloud.example.com) Click "Log in" -- this opens the Login Flow in your browser Grant access in the browser Choose which folders to sync NextCloud Android Install from F-Droid or Google Play Enter your Cog server URL Authenticate via Login Flow Auto-upload photos and access files NextCloud iOS Install from the App Store Enter your Cog server URL Authenticate via Login Flow DAVx5 (Android) For CalDAV and CardDAV sync on Android: Install DAVx5 Add account with your Cog server URL Enter username and app password DAVx5 discovers calendars and address books automatically Thunderbird Calendar Go to Calendar > New Calendar > On the Network Enter: https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/calendars/<username>/ Enter username and app password Contacts (CardBook add-on) Install the CardBook add-on Add a new remote address book Enter: https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/addressbooks/<username>/ Enter credentials Apple Calendar & Contacts (macOS/iOS) System Settings > Internet Accounts > Add Other Account Choose CalDAV or CardDAV Server: cloud.example.com Username and app password Apple clients use /.well-known/caldav and /.well-known/carddav for automatic discovery. GNOME Online Accounts Settings > Online Accounts > NextCloud Enter your Cog server URL and credentials Calendar, contacts, and files sync automatically Floccus (Browser Bookmark Sync) Install the Floccus browser extension Choose "NextCloud Bookmarks" as the adapter Enter your Cog server URL and credentials Bookmarks sync bidirectionally RSS Reader Apps Apps compatible with the NextCloud News API: NextCloud News (Android/iOS) FeedMe (Android) Newsboat (with NextCloud News plugin) API endpoint: https://cloud.example.com/index.php/apps/news/api/v1-2/

title: Login Flow v2
text: Login Flow v2 Login Flow v2 is the mechanism NextCloud clients use to authenticate without directly handling passwords. Cog implements this protocol for compatibility with NextCloud desktop and mobile clients. How it works Client initiates -- the client sends POST /index.php/login/v2 to the server Server responds with a poll token and a grant URL User authenticates -- the client opens the grant URL in a browser, the user logs in and clicks "Grant Access" Client polls -- the client polls POST /index.php/login/v2/poll with the token Server responds with an app password and the login name on success The generated app password is a long-lived credential the client uses for all subsequent requests (WebDAV, OCS, etc.). Endpoints Method Path Description POST /index.php/login/v2 Initiate login flow POST /index.php/login/v2/poll Poll for completion GET /index.php/login/v2/grant Grant page (browser) POST /index.php/login/v2/grant Confirm grant (browser) Timeout Login flow sessions expire after 10 minutes. If the user doesn't grant access within that time, the client must start a new flow. Troubleshooting Client can't connect: Ensure COG_BASE_URL is set correctly and accessible from the client Grant page doesn't load: Check reverse proxy configuration -- the grant URL must be reachable from the user's browser Poll returns nothing: The user hasn't granted access yet, or the session expired

title: NextCloud Compatibility
text: NextCloud Compatibility Cog implements a subset of NextCloud APIs to provide compatibility with the NextCloud ecosystem of clients and apps. Supported APIs API Status Used by WebDAV Files Supported Desktop/mobile sync, file managers CalDAV Supported Calendar clients (Thunderbird, Apple Calendar, DAVx5) CardDAV Supported Contact clients (Apple Contacts, DAVx5, Thunderbird) OCS Capabilities Supported All NextCloud clients (server feature discovery) OCS User Info Supported Desktop/mobile clients OCS Sharing Supported Desktop/mobile sharing UI Login Flow v2 Supported Desktop/mobile client authentication Chunked Upload v2 Supported Desktop client large file uploads Direct Download Tokens Supported Client preview generation News API v1-2 Supported RSS reader apps Bookmarks API v2 Supported Bookmark sync (Floccus) Memories API Supported NextCloud Memories photo app Not implemented Server-side encryption APIs Activity/notification APIs Talk/messaging APIs Deck/project management APIs Text/collaborative editing APIs Endpoints Status: GET /status.php Capabilities: GET /ocs/v1.php/cloud/capabilities WebDAV: /remote.php/dav/files/<username>/ CalDAV: /remote.php/dav/calendars/<username>/ CardDAV: /remote.php/dav/addressbooks/<username>/ See Clients for setup instructions for specific apps.

title: CLI Commands
text: CLI Commands Plugins can register commands that appear under cog <plugin-id> in the CLI. Registering a command This creates cog rss scan (assuming the plugin ID is "rss"). CommandDef Positional arguments Specify expected arguments by name. The CLI enforces the exact count: Usage: cog bookmarks import bookmarks.html Subcommands Use Sub for command groups. Run and Sub are mutually exclusive: Usage: cog rss feeds list, cog rss feeds add https://example.com/feed.xml

title: Custom Builds
text: Custom Builds You can build a custom Cog binary that includes additional plugins alongside the built-in ones. Using cog.Main The simplest approach -- provides the full CLI (serve, user, group, volume, shell, doctor): The protected plugins (Dashboard and Files) are always included automatically. Your plugins are added alongside the built-in ones. Using cog.Run For more control over the server lifecycle: Config When using cog.Main, config is read from environment variables. When using cog.Run, you provide the config directly. The standard build The default cmd/cog/main.go is a minimal custom build that includes all built-in plugins: You can use this as a template and add your own plugins to the list.

title: Getting Started with Plugin Development
headings: Wire it into a custom build
text: Getting Started with Plugin Development This guide walks through building a minimal Cog plugin from scratch. The Plugin interface Every plugin implements four methods: ID -- unique string identifier (e.g. "myplugin") Register -- declare routes, resources, nav items, widgets, etc. Start -- begin background work (called after all plugins register) Stop -- clean up on shutdown Minimal example Create a new Go module for your plugin: Create hello.go: Wire it into a custom build Create cmd/cog-custom/main.go: The built-in plugins (Dashboard, Files, Calendar, etc.) are automatically included. Your plugin is added alongside them. Build and run: Visit http://localhost:8580 and you'll see "Hello" in the navigation bar. Adding a database Most plugins need per-user data storage. Cog provides SQLite databases automatically. Create sql/schema.sql: Embed it and run migrations in Register: See Databases for the full database guide. Adding a dashboard widget Adding search See Search Indexing for making your plugin's data searchable. Next steps Plugin Interface -- full reference for Plugin and optional interfaces Registration -- all Registrar methods Databases -- per-user and root databases, migrations Custom Builds -- building custom Cog distributions gRPC Plugins -- building out-of-process plugins

title: Plugin Databases
text: Plugin Databases Cog provides SQLite databases for plugin data storage. Each plugin gets isolated databases that are automatically created and managed. Per-user databases Each plugin gets a separate SQLite database per user, stored at: Access the database during request handling: Databases are opened in WAL mode with foreign keys enabled. Root database For plugin-wide state shared across all users (e.g. feed poll schedules, global configuration), use the root database: Stored at app_data/{plugin_id}/root.db. Schema migrations Use plugin.Migrate() to manage your database schema. Create an embedded filesystem with SQL files: Embed and run: schema.sql Contains the full current schema using CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS. This is the canonical schema definition. Migration files Named migration*.sql and run in order after the schema. For adding columns or modifying existing tables. Guard comments Migration files support conditional execution: The migration only runs if the specified column does not exist, preventing errors on repeated execution. Best practices Use plugin.Migrate() for all schema management -- don't run raw DDL Keep write transactions small and bounded Use prepared statements for repeated queries Remember that each user has a separate database -- there are no cross-user joins For cross-user data, use the root database or the share system

title: Plugin Interface Reference
text: Plugin Interface Reference Plugin The core interface every plugin must implement. ID Returns the plugin's unique identifier. Used for route prefixes (/apps/{id}/), database paths, CLI namespacing, and resource type prefixes. Convention: lowercase, alphanumeric, no spaces (e.g. "files", "calendar", "bookmarks"). Register Called during startup. Use the PluginContext (which embeds Registrar) to declare routes, resources, nav items, widgets, search sources, and hooks. Also access services like PluginDB(), Logger(), and ShareStore(). Start Called after all plugins have registered. Use this for background goroutines (polling, scanning, etc.). The context is cancelled on shutdown. Stop Called during shutdown for cleanup. Return after all background work has stopped. Optional interfaces Doctor Contribute health checks to cog doctor. FolderIconProvider Provide custom folder icons in the file browser. Return inline SVG markup for folders your plugin manages (e.g. the Gallery plugin might show a camera icon for "Photos/"). Lifecycle Load -- plugin struct is created (e.g. New()) Register -- plugin declares its routes, resources, and hooks Start -- plugin begins background work Run -- plugin serves requests Stop -- plugin shuts down gracefully

title: Plugin System Overview
text: Plugin System Overview Cog's plugin system allows developers to extend the platform with new apps, protocols, and integrations. Plugins can register web pages, API endpoints, dashboard widgets, navigation items, CLI commands, search sources, shareable resources, and WebDAV handlers. Trust tiers Plugins fall into four trust tiers: Tier Language Isolation Route scope Disable Examples Protected Go (in-process) None Global No Dashboard, Files Privileged Go (in-process) None Global Yes Calendar, Contacts Trusted Go or gRPC Process (gRPC) /apps/{id}/ Yes 3rd-party plugins External Any (gRPC) Process + iframe /apps/{id}/ Yes User-installed Protected plugins are always on and cannot be disabled by admins. Privileged plugins run in-process and can bind routes outside their /apps/{id}/ prefix. Trusted plugins can be Go (compiled in) or gRPC (separate process). Routes are scoped to their prefix. External plugins run as separate processes and are sandboxed. Package layout The module path is git.duckfam.us/jj-software/cog. Import the plugin package as: Next steps Getting Started -- build your first plugin Plugin Interface -- full interface reference Registration -- routes, nav items, widgets, and more

title: Registration
text: Registration During Register(), plugins use the Registrar interface to declare their capabilities. Pages Mounts a GET handler at /apps/{plugin_id}/{path}. The handler renders an HTML content fragment -- the navigation bar, head, and scripts are wrapped automatically by middleware. Use {$} as the path for the plugin's root page. The request context contains the authenticated user and CSRF token: API endpoints Mounts a GET handler at /apps/{plugin_id}/{path} for JSON or HTMX partial responses. Auth-wrapped (returns 401 on failure, not a redirect). Actions Mounts a state-changing handler (POST, PUT, or DELETE) at /apps/{plugin_id}/{path}. Automatically wrapped with auth and CSRF protection. For form submissions, use the Post-Redirect-Get pattern: process the form, set a flash message, and redirect with 303. Navigation items Adds an entry to the top navigation bar. Nav items from disabled plugins are automatically excluded. Dashboard widgets Adds a widget to the dashboard. The Render function writes HTML directly to the writer. Keep widget rendering fast -- there is no timeout enforcement. Hooks Subscribe to named events. Hook callbacks receive a context and event data: WebDAV handlers Mounts a handler under /remote.php/dav/{prefix}/. The handler receives authenticated requests with the full path. Used for CalDAV, CardDAV, and custom DAV endpoints. Settings pages Adds an admin settings page for the plugin. See Settings Pages for details. CLI commands Registers a CLI command available as cog <plugin-id> <command>. See CLI Commands for details. Search sources Registers a database table for full-text indexing. See Search Indexing for details. Shareable resources Declares a resource type that users can share. See Sharing Resources for details.

title: Search Indexing
text: Search Indexing Plugins can make their data searchable by registering a search source. Cog maintains a per-user Bleve full-text index that is updated asynchronously. Registering a search source SearchSourceDef PrimaryTable The SQLite table to watch for changes. Cog uses SQLite update hooks to detect inserts, updates, and deletes on this table and triggers re-indexing automatically. EnrichSQL A SELECT query that fetches the data to index. Requirements: Must return rowid as the first column Must contain WHERE rowid IN (?) as a placeholder Remaining columns are mapped by position: Column 1 (after rowid) → name -- the primary display text in search results Column 2 → subtext -- secondary display text Remaining columns → content -- concatenated for full-text indexing ContentFunc (optional) For internal plugins that need to extract file content (e.g. the Files plugin reading text from files on disk). Receives the user's files directory path and all SQL column values as a map. Return "" to skip content indexing for a row. How indexing works Cog installs SQLite update hooks on the PrimaryTable in each user's plugin database When a row is inserted, updated, or deleted, the change is queued The search manager batches changes and runs EnrichSQL to fetch the current data Data is indexed into the user's Bleve index Deletions are automatically handled -- if EnrichSQL returns no rows for a rowid, the document is removed from the index Indexing is eventually consistent -- there is a brief delay between a change and its appearance in search results. Example: Bookmarks plugin This indexes bookmarks with the title as the display name, URL as subtext, and description + page content as searchable text.

title: Settings Pages
text: Settings Pages Plugins can register admin settings pages for configuration. Registering a settings page SettingsPage Slug The URL segment for the page. Empty string means this is the plugin's default settings page. Non-empty slugs create additional pages (e.g. "recognition" becomes /admin/plugins/{id}/recognition). Name Display name in the settings sidebar. If empty, the plugin's display name is used. Handler Renders the page content fragment on GET. The HTML shell (sidebar, navigation) is wrapped automatically. Action Handles POST form submissions. Use the Post-Redirect-Get pattern: process the form, set a flash message, and redirect with 303. Sidebar navigation The sidebar entry depends on how many pages the plugin registers: Single page, no name -- shows as just the plugin name (e.g. "RSS") Single page, with name -- shows as "Plugin: Name" (e.g. "RSS: Feeds") Multiple pages -- displayed as a nested group under the plugin name. A page with empty slug becomes the overview. Multiple settings pages Settings pages are admin-only -- regular users cannot access them.

title: Sharing Resources
text: Sharing Resources Plugins can register resource types that users can share with other users, groups, or via public links. Registering a resource ResourceDef The full resource type is formed as {plugin_id}:{type} (e.g. bookmarks:folder, calendar:calendar). ParentColumn If set, sharing a parent resource implicitly grants access to all children. For example, sharing a directory grants access to files inside it. Cog walks the parent hierarchy when checking access. Handler Serves requests when a user accesses a specific resource (e.g. from a search result or shared link): Use ResourceHandlerFunc to adapt a function. PermissionLevels If empty, defaults to "Read-only" (PermRead) and "Read/Write" (PermRead | PermWrite). Permission constants Accessing the share store Use ShareStore() from PluginContext for programmatic share operations: How cross-user access works When User B accesses a resource owned by User A: Cog checks the global shares table for User B's access (direct, group, or instance shares) If authorized, Cog invokes the plugin with a connection to User A's database The request context includes the resource IDs and permissions User B has The plugin doesn't need to implement sharing logic -- Cog handles the access control and database scoping.

title: gRPC Plugins
text: gRPC Plugins External plugins run as separate processes and communicate with Cog over gRPC on a Unix socket. Building a gRPC plugin Create a standard Go binary that calls plugcmd.Run(): Build it as a standalone binary: How it works Cog creates a temporary Unix socket Cog launches your binary with COG_PLUGIN_SOCKET set to the socket path Your process serves plugpb.PluginService on that socket — in Go, plugcmd.Run() does this Cog connects and calls GetID to learn the plugin ID Cog calls Register, which streams registration events (routes, nav items, widgets, etc.) HTTP requests to your routes are proxied over gRPC The protocol is the contract, not the Go SDK: any language that can serve plugin/plugpb/plugin.proto over a Unix socket can be a plugin. The examples here are Go because plugcmd is what the tree ships. Supported registrations The following work over gRPC: RegisterPage -- pages are proxied as HTTP requests RegisterAPI -- API endpoints are proxied RegisterAction -- actions are proxied with CSRF handling RegisterNavItem -- navigation entries RegisterWidget -- dashboard widgets (rendered via gRPC call) RegisterHook -- hook subscriptions (fire-and-forget) RegisterResource -- shareable resources Limitations The following are not available to gRPC plugins: Feature Reason PluginDB() Database access is not proxied over gRPC RootDB() Same UserFilesDir() Filesystem paths are not meaningful across processes UserVFS() VFS is not proxied RegisterDAVHandler() No-op for gRPC plugins RegisterSettingsPage() No-op for gRPC plugins RegisterCommand() No-op for gRPC plugins RegisterSearchSource() Not yet supported over gRPC ShareStore() Returns nil EmailSender() Returns nil CSRFSecret() Returns nil gRPC plugins should use their registered API/action routes for all data access, or manage their own local storage. Installation Place compiled plugin binaries in /var/lib/cog/plugins/. The Cog host discovers and loads them via Registry.LoadExternal(). Process isolation A gRPC plugin is a process that serves plugpb.PluginService on the socket named by COG_PLUGIN_SOCKET. Nothing about that requires Go or an import of Cog; plugcmd is one implementation of the server side, and everything in this section applies to any other. What the host does It captures your output. The host reads the process's stdout and stderr and re-emits them line by line through its own logger, attributed to your plugin ID — stdout at INFO, stderr at ERROR. A crash message therefore reaches the admin log viewer (Admin → Logs) and not just the host's stderr. Two consequences worth designing around: write ordinary logs to stdout, because anything on stderr is recorded as an error regardless of what you think its level is; and write a line at a time, because that is the unit the host logs. Structured output is not parsed — a JSON log line is recorded as its text. It restarts a process that exits. The host waits on the process, and when it exits — cleanly or not — relaunches it on a fresh socket, backing off from 1s to a maximum of 30s between attempts, and keeps trying until the server shuts down. While the plugin is down its routes answer 503 with a short "temporarily unavailable" page instead of leaking a dial error to the browser. A request that fails for any other reason gets a 500. Either way the underlying status is logged, not rendered. It requires you to come back the same. Routes are mounted on the host's mux once, at load, and cannot be remounted, so a restarted process must be the plugin the host already mounted routes for: GetID must return the same ID it returned before. Register is called again on the new connection, and must stream the same route keys, in the same order, as the first time. The host uses the stream to let you rebuild your own route table; it does not re-mount anything from it. Generate route keys from something stable — the route itself, or a fixed registration order — not from a clock, a random source, or anything that varies with external state. A process that comes back with different keys is refused and the failure logged as a restart rejection, because the alternative is dispatching requests to whichever handler now happens to hold the old key. It does not detect a wedged plugin. Only exits are noticed. A process that stays up and stops answering keeps its routes. What your process must do Do not let one request end the process. A fault in a handler should be caught and returned as a gRPC error — INTERNAL is what the host renders as a 500 — rather than propagating out and terminating the server. This matters more here than in an ordinary service: the host holds the path of the socket you were listening on, so a process that dies mid-request takes every one of its routes down until the supervisor gets it back. In Go, plugcmd.Run does this for you with recovery interceptors on both the unary and streaming methods. That covers panics raised while serving a request. It cannot cover a panic in a goroutine you started yourself — nothing outside that goroutine can recover it — so recover in your own goroutines. An implementation in another language needs the equivalent guard at its own service boundary. Expect to be killed, and to be orphaned. The host kills the process when it shuts down cleanly. If the host itself is killed, nothing does: the plugin is left running with a socket directory under /tmp that no one will connect to again. Hold no state that a sudden exit would corrupt, and treat a fresh start as the normal case rather than the exceptional one.
